subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 2(7) - Consumer Definition & Commercial Purpose Exclusion
question: Apex Heavy Machinery Pvt. Ltd. purchases an industrial generator costing ₹35 Lakhs for use in its automotive manufacturing plant. The generator breaks down repeatedly due to manufacturing defects. Apex Heavy Machinery files a complaint before the State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Can Apex Heavy Machinery maintain the complaint as a 'consumer'?
options: No, because under Section 2(7) of CPA 2019, a person who obtains goods for 'commercial purpose' is excluded from the definition of a consumer (unless purchased exclusively for earning livelihood by means of self-employment).
Yes, any entity that pays consideration is unconditionally a consumer under CPA 2019.
Yes, provided the complaint is supported by a technical engineer's affidavit.
Companies are never permitted to file consumer complaints under any circumstances.
ref: Section 2(7)(i) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 2(7)(i) of CPA 2019, 'consumer' means any person who buys any goods for a consideration, but DOES NOT INCLUDE a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose. Under the Explanation, 'commercial purpose' does not include use by a person of goods bought and used by him exclusively for the purpose of earning his livelihood by means of self-employment. An industrial company purchasing machinery for manufacturing is excluded.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 - Pecuniary Jurisdiction of Consumer Commissions
question: Under the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission) Rules, 2021, what are the pecuniary jurisdictions of the District Commission, State Commission, and National Commission based on value of goods/services paid as consideration?
options: District Commission: Value up to ₹50 Lakhs; State Commission: Value exceeding ₹50 Lakhs up to ₹2 Crores; National Commission: Value exceeding ₹2 Crores.
District: up to ₹1 Crore; State: ₹1 Cr to ₹10 Cr; National: above ₹10 Cr.
District: up to ₹20 Lakhs; State: ₹20 Lakhs to ₹1 Cr; National: above ₹1 Cr.
District: up to ₹5 Lakhs; State: ₹5 Lakhs to ₹50 Lakhs; National: above ₹50 Lakhs.
ref: Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction of the District, State and National Commission) Rules, 2021 (Notification dated 30.12.2021)
explanation: By the 2021 Rules revising pecuniary jurisdiction under CPA 2019: District Commission entertains complaints where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed ₹50 Lakhs; State Commission where consideration exceeds ₹50 Lakhs but does not exceed ₹2 Crores; National Commission where consideration exceeds ₹2 Crores.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 82 to 87 - Product Liability
question: A consumer purchases a pressure cooker from an authorized retail shop. Due to a defect in the safety valve manufactured with substandard alloy, the cooker explodes, causing severe burn injuries to the consumer and property damage to the kitchen. Under Chapter VI (Product Liability) of CPA, 2019, who can be held liable in a product liability action?
options: A product liability action may be brought against a product manufacturer, product service provider or product seller, as the case may be, for any harm caused by a defective product under Section 82.
Only the retail shopkeeper who handed the box to the customer.
No product liability action can be initiated unless criminal charges of murder are framed.
Liability is limited strictly to the replacement of the pressure cooker with no damages for physical harm.
ref: Section 82, 84 and 86 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 82 of CPA 2019, a product liability action may be brought by a complainant against a product manufacturer or a product service provider or a product seller, as the case may be, for any harm caused by a defective product. Under Section 84, a product manufacturer is liable if the product contains a manufacturing defect, design defect, or lacks adequate instructions/warnings.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 10 & 21 - CCPA Powers & Celebrity Endorsement Liability
question: Under Section 10 and 21 of CPA, 2019, what power does the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) possess regarding misleading advertisements and celebrity endorsers?
options: CCPA can direct withdrawal/modification of misleading ads, impose penalties up to ₹10 Lakhs (and up to ₹50 Lakhs for subsequent contravention) on manufacturers/endorsers, and prohibit an endorser from endorsing that product/service for up to 1 year (extendable up to 3 years).
CCPA can only issue non-binding recommendations to the Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI).
Celebrity endorsers have absolute statutory immunity from prosecution.
CCPA can revoke the citizenship of celebrity endorsers.
ref: Section 21(1), 21(2) and 21(3) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 21 of CPA 2019, the CCPA may impose a penalty up to ₹10 Lakhs on a manufacturer or endorser for false/misleading advertisement (up to ₹50 Lakhs for subsequent violations), and prohibit the endorser of a false or misleading advertisement from making endorsement of any product or service for a period which may extend to one year (up to 3 years for subsequent violations). Endorser is exempt if he carried out due diligence.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 69 - Limitation Period for Filing Complaint
question: Under Section 69 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, what is the limitation period within which a complaint must be filed before the District Commission, State Commission, or National Commission?
options: Within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen (condonable if sufficient cause is shown).
Within one year from the date of purchase of the product.
Within 90 days from the date of issuing notice to the seller.
Within 3 years as per the general Limitation Act, 1963.
ref: Section 69(1) and 69(2) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 69(1), the District Commission, the State Commission or the National Commission shall not admit a complaint unless it is filed within two years from the date on which the cause of action has arisen. Under Section 69(2), a complaint may be entertained after two years if the complainant satisfies the Commission that he had sufficient cause for not filing within period.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 41, 51 & 67 - Appeals & Pre-Deposit Requirement
question: An order is passed by the State Commission directing a builder to refund ₹80 Lakhs to a homebuyer. The builder intends to file an appeal before the National Commission under Section 51. What pre-deposit condition must the builder satisfy before the appeal can be entertained?
options: The builder must deposit fifty percent (50%) of the amount ordered by the State Commission before the National Commission can entertain the appeal.
Deposit of ₹25,000 only.
Deposit of 100% of the awarded amount plus interest.
Zero deposit is required for filing an appeal under CPA 2019.
ref: Second proviso to Section 51(1) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under the second proviso to Section 51(1), no appeal by a person who is required to pay any amount in terms of an order of the State Commission shall be entertained by the National Commission unless the appellant has deposited fifty per cent (50%) of that amount in the prescribed manner. Similar 50% pre-deposit rules apply to appeals from District to State Commission (Sec 41) and from National Commission to Supreme Court (Sec 67).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 3 & 4 - Offence of Money Laundering & Punishment
question: Under Section 3 and 4 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), whosoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge or knowingly assists or knowingly is a party in any process connected with the proceeds of crime is guilty of money laundering. What is the statutory punishment prescribed under Section 4?
options: Rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than 3 years but which may extend to 7 years (and up to 10 years if the scheduled offence is under the NDPS Act) and fine.
Simple imprisonment up to 1 year and fine up to ₹1 Lakh.
Monetary fine only with zero prison sentence.
Detention in civil prison for 6 months.
ref: Section 4 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 4, any person who commits the offence of money-laundering shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine. Where the proceeds of crime involved relate to any offence specified under paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule (NDPS Act), the imprisonment may extend to ten years.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 5 - Attachment of Property Involved in Money Laundering
question: Under Section 5(1) of PMLA, 2002, the Director or any officer not below the rank of Deputy Director may provisionally attach property involved in money laundering. What is the maximum validity period of such provisional attachment order before confirmation by the Adjudicating Authority?
options: For a period not exceeding 180 days from the date of the order.
For a period of 30 days only.
For 1 year automatically.
Indefinitely until completion of criminal trial.
ref: Section 5(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 5(1), where the Director or any officer not below the rank of Deputy Director has reason to believe that any person is in possession of proceeds of crime, he may by order in writing provisionally attach such property for a period not exceeding 180 days from the date of the order. The attachment must be confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 8.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 12 - Reporting Entities & Client Verification (KYC)
question: Under Section 12 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, every reporting entity (including banking companies, financial institutions, intermediaries, and designated professionals) must maintain records of all transactions for what minimum duration?
options: For a period of five years from the date of transaction between a client and the reporting entity, and maintain records of identity of clients for five years after the business relationship has ended.
For a period of two years from the audit date.
For eight years under the Companies Act rules.
Records must be permanently preserved indefinitely.
ref: Section 12(1)(a) and Section 12(3) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 12(3) of PMLA, records of transactions referred to in clause (a) of sub-section (1) shall be maintained for a period of five years from the date of transaction between a client and the reporting entity. Under Section 12(4), records of identity of clients and account files shall be maintained for a period of five years after the business relationship has ended or account closed.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 24 - Burden of Proof in Money Laundering
question: Under Section 24 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, in any proceeding relating to proceeds of crime, upon whom does the burden of proof lie with respect to property being untainted?
options: In the case of a person charged with the offence of money-laundering under section 3, the Authority or Court shall presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money-laundering, and the burden of proving that the property is untainted lies on the accused.
The prosecution (Enforcement Directorate) must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt without any statutory presumption.
The burden of proof shifts to the commercial bank where funds were deposited.
Burden of proof lies on the statutory auditor who certified the balance sheet.
ref: Section 24(a) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. UOI)
explanation: Under Section 24(a) of PMLA, 2002, in the case of a person charged with the offence of money-laundering under section 3, the Authority or Court shall presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money-laundering. The burden of proof is reversed and placed on the accused to establish that the property is untainted (upheld by Supreme Court in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 35 - Manner in Which Complaint Shall be Made
question: Under Section 35(1) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a complaint in relation to any goods sold or delivered or agreed to be sold or delivered or any service provided or agreed to be provided may be filed with a District Commission by:
options: The consumer, or any recognized consumer association, or one or more consumers having same interest (class action), or the Central Government, CCPA or State Government.
Only the individual consumer personally; associations cannot file complaints.
Only an advocate registered with the State Bar Council.
Only after obtaining a certificate of conciliation from the local police.
ref: Section 35(1) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 35(1), a complaint may be filed by: (a) the consumer to whom goods are sold or service provided; (b) any recognized consumer association; (c) one or more consumers, where there are numerous consumers having the same interest (class action); (d) the Central Government, the Central Authority (CCPA) or the State Government.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 34(2) - Place of Filing Complaint (Consumer Convenience)
question: Under Section 34(2) of CPA, 2019, can a complainant file a consumer complaint before the District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the complainant resides or personally works for gain?
options: Yes, CPA 2019 introduced an explicit provision allowing the complainant to file the complaint where the complainant resides or personally works for gain (in addition to where the opposite party resides or cause of action arises).
No, the complaint can only be filed where the registered office of the seller is situated.
No, the complaint must be filed in New Delhi before the National Commission.
Only if the seller gives written consent to the jurisdiction.
ref: Section 34(2)(d) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 34(2)(d), a complaint shall be instituted in a District Commission within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the complainant resides or personally works for gain. This is a major pro-consumer reform compared to the 1986 Act which required filing at the defendant's place.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Chapter V - Consumer Mediation Cells
question: Under Chapter V (Mediation) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, where does the Consumer Commission refer the parties for settlement if it appears that there exists elements of a settlement acceptable to the parties?
options: To the Consumer Mediation Cell established attached to the District, State or National Commission, with the written consent of both parties within 5 days.
To the local Gram Panchayat for customary arbitration.
To the High Court Lok Adalat compulsorily.
Mediation is prohibited in consumer disputes.
ref: Section 37(1) and Section 74 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 37(1), at the first hearing of the complaint after admission, or at any later stage, if it appears to the District Commission that there exist elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties, it may direct the parties to give written consent within five days to refer the matter for settlement through mediation, and upon receiving consent, refer the matter to the Consumer Mediation Cell attached to that Commission.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 44 - Offences Triable by Special Courts
question: Under Section 44(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, which court has exclusive jurisdiction to try an offence punishable under Section 4 of PMLA and any scheduled offence connected to it?
options: The Special Court constituted for the area in which the offence has been committed, designated by the Central Government in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court.
The Court of Metropolitan Magistrate.
The National Company Law Tribunal.
The Armed Forces Tribunal.
ref: Section 43 and Section 44(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 43(1), the Central Government, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court, designates one or more Courts of Session as Special Court(s). Under Section 44(1), an offence punishable under section 4 and any scheduled offence connected to the offence under that section shall be triable by the Special Court constituted for the area in which the offence has been committed.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 45 - Twin Conditions for Bail (Strict Bail Norms)
question: Under Section 45(1) of PMLA, 2002 (as upheld by the Supreme Court), what 'twin conditions' must be satisfied before a person accused of an offence of money laundering can be released on bail?
options: The Public Prosecutor must be given an opportunity to oppose bail, and where the Public Prosecutor opposes, the Court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
The accused must deposit 100% of the disputed proceeds of crime in cash with the Enforcement Directorate.
The accused must surrender all foreign passports and promise to appear once a year.
Bail is an absolute right under PMLA and no special conditions apply.
ref: Section 45(1) of PMLA, 2002 read with Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India (SC 2022)
explanation: Under Section 45(1) of PMLA, no person accused of an offence under this Act shall be released on bail unless: (i) the Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application; and (ii) where the Public Prosecutor opposes the application, the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 2(47) - Unfair Trade Practice Definition
question: Under Section 2(47) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, which of the following practices is explicitly categorized as an 'Unfair Trade Practice'?
options: Refusal to issue a cash memo or bill for goods sold or services rendered, or disclosing a consumer's personal information without consent, or offering gifts or prizes without intention of providing them.
Offering genuine discounts during festive seasonal clearance sales.
Selling goods strictly at or below Maximum Retail Price (MRP).
Displaying bilingual ingredients list on food packages.
ref: Section 2(47)(vii), (viii), (ix) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 2(47) of CPA 2019, unfair trade practices include: not issuing a bill or cash memo (clause vii); refusing to take back defective goods or refund consideration within period stipulated in bill (clause viii); and disclosing to other persons any personal information given in confidence by the consumer unless made in accordance with law (clause ix).

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 90 - Punishment for Manufacturing/Selling Adulterated Goods
question: Under Section 90(1)(c) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, if a person manufactures for sale or stores, sells or distributes any adulterant or adulterated product which causes the death of a consumer, what punishment is prescribed?
options: Imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than 7 years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and with fine which shall not be less than ₹10 Lakhs.
Simple imprisonment up to 6 months and fine of ₹20,000.
Warning letter and temporary sealing of shop for 3 days.
Mandatory community service for 100 hours.
ref: Section 90(1)(d) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 90(1)(d), where the adulterant or adulterated product causes the death of a consumer, the person responsible shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years, but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and with fine which shall not be less than ten lakh rupees.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] PMLA 2002 Sec 17 - Search and Seizure Authority
question: Under Section 17 of PMLA, 2002, who authorizes an authorized officer to enter and search any building, place, vessel, vehicle or aircraft and seize records and property involved in money laundering?
options: The Director or an officer not below the rank of Deputy Director authorized by him, who on the basis of information in his possession has reason to believe (recorded in writing) that a person has committed an act of money laundering.
The President of the local Municipal Corporation.
A judicial magistrate through a bailable warrant.
The Registrar of Companies.
ref: Section 17(1) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002
explanation: Under Section 17(1), where the Director or any other officer not below the rank of Deputy Director authorised by him for the purposes of this section, on the basis of information in his possession, has reason to believe (the reason for such belief to be recorded in writing) that any person has committed any act which constitutes money-laundering, or is in possession of any proceeds of crime, he may authorise any officer subordinate to him to enter, search and seize.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] CPA 2019 Sec 71 & 72 - Enforcement of Orders & Penalties for Failure
question: If a person fails to comply with any order made by the District Commission, State Commission or National Commission under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, what punishment can the Commission impose under Section 72?
options: Imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one month, but which may extend to three years, or with fine, which shall not be less than ₹25,000, but which may extend to ₹1 Lakh, or with both.
Disqualification from voting in Lok Sabha elections.
Simple fine of ₹500 without imprisonment.
The Commission has no enforcement powers and must file a fresh suit in a Civil Court.
ref: Section 72(1) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
explanation: Under Section 72(1), whoever fails to comply with any order made by the District Commission or the State Commission or the National Commission, as the case may be, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one month, but which may extend to three years, or with fine, which shall not be less than twenty-five thousand rupees, but which may extend to one lakh rupees, or with both.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
topicTitle: Consumer protection and other economic legislation
tag: [ICAI CA Final PYQ] Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 (FEOA) - Key Threshold
question: Under the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 (related economic legislation), what is the minimum value threshold of economic offences specified in the Schedule for an individual to be declared a 'Fugitive Economic Offender'?
options: Total value involved in the economic offences or offences must be ₹100 Crores or more, and the individual has left India to avoid criminal prosecution or refuses to return to India to face prosecution.
Value of offence exceeds ₹10 Crores.
Value of offence exceeds ₹500 Crores.
Any bouncing of cheque under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
ref: Section 2(1)(f) of the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018
explanation: Under Section 2(1)(f) of the FEOA, 2018, 'fugitive economic offender' means any individual against whom a warrant for arrest in relation to a scheduled offence has been issued by any Court in India, who: (i) has left India so as to avoid criminal prosecution; or (ii) being abroad, refuses to return to India to face criminal prosecution, AND the total value involved in such offence or offences is ₹100 Crores or more.
